scenarios.title: Pick a license
scenarios.situation: You are publishing a small utility library you wrote. You want maximum adoption, including by commercial products, and you do not want to police how people use it.
choices: A permissive license such as MIT or Apache-2.0, which allows commercial use with minimal obligations
No license at all, which keeps things simple and still lets people use it
A strong copyleft license, to force improvements back to the community
A custom license you write yourself with exactly the terms you want
scenarios.why: No license means no permission: by default others have no rights to use, modify, or distribute your code, which kills adoption. Permissive licenses (MIT, Apache-2.0) grant broad rights with only attribution required, matching your goal. Custom licenses create legal uncertainty that companies avoid.
scenarios.hint: What rights does the public have to your code if you publish with no license file?

scenarios.title: The README test
scenarios.situation: A developer lands on your project's page from a search result. You have 30 seconds of their attention. Your README currently opens with a 2,000-word architecture essay.
scenarios.prompt: What belongs at the top of the README?
choices: What the project does in one or two sentences, then install and quick-start commands that work by copy-paste
The full architecture essay, since understanding the design matters most
A long list of planned features to show ambition
Contributor biographies, to establish credibility
scenarios.why: READMEs are read top-down by impatient strangers: the first screen must answer 'what is this' and 'how do I try it' with commands that actually run. Architecture essays, roadmaps, and bios belong further down or in docs/. If the quick-start fails, nothing else in the README matters.
scenarios.hint: What does a visitor need in the first 30 seconds to decide to try it?

scenarios.title: The 4,000-line PR
scenarios.situation: A contributor opens a pull request with 4,000 changed lines: a refactor, two features, and a dependency upgrade, all in one. CI passes. You are the maintainer and review time is scarce.
choices: Ask them to split it into small, independently reviewable PRs: refactor alone, then each feature, then the upgrade
Merge it since CI passes; green checks mean it is safe
Close it as too big without review to teach them a lesson
Review it line by line over the next two weeks
scenarios.why: CI passing proves the code compiles and tests pass, not that the change is correct, safe, or desirable. Large mixed PRs are unreviewable in practice: reviewers skim, real issues hide, and reverts become all-or-nothing. Small stacked PRs get real review, bisect cleanly, and revert independently.
scenarios.hint: If this PR introduces a bug, how precisely can you revert just the bad part?

scenarios.title: The unlicensed dependency
scenarios.situation: You find a perfect library for your project: it does exactly what you need and is actively maintained. Its repository has no LICENSE file, and the author has not responded to your issue asking about licensing in three weeks.
choices: Do not ship it in your project; find an alternative with a clear license or write the functionality yourself
Use it anyway; public code on the internet is free to use
Use it but rewrite it slightly so it counts as your own work
Fork it and add an MIT license yourself since the author seems friendly
scenarios.why: Code without a license grants you no rights: using it exposes your project (and employer) to infringement claims. Rewriting 'slightly' does not clean the rights, and you cannot license someone else's work. The safe paths are a licensed alternative, a clean-room implementation, or waiting for the author's explicit grant.
scenarios.hint: Who has the legal power to grant you rights to this code?

scenarios.title: The breaking release
scenarios.situation: Your library has 2,000 users. You need to rename a widely used function and change its argument order to fix a design flaw. Users pin versions loosely (many use ^1.x ranges).
scenarios.prompt: How do you ship this responsibly?
choices: Ship it as a major version (2.0.0) with migration notes, keep the old API working with a deprecation warning for one minor release cycle first if feasible
Ship it as 1.5.0 since it is 'just' a rename; semver is a guideline
Rename it silently in a patch release and document it in the changelog
Never change it; the design flaw is permanent now
scenarios.why: Semantic versioning is a contract: major means breaking, minor means additive, patch means fixes. Users on ^1.x ranges auto-update into anything below 2.0.0, so a breaking rename in a minor silently breaks builds downstream. A deprecation period plus a major bump with migration notes respects that contract.
scenarios.hint: What does the ^ in your users' version ranges promise them?

scenarios.title: The burned-out maintainer
scenarios.situation: You maintain a popular open-source tool solo. Issues pile up, a company depends on it commercially, and you are exhausted. A stranger offers to 'take it over' via a one-line email.
scenarios.prompt: What is the responsible path forward?
choices: Slow down deliberately: document the situation, recruit co-maintainers gradually with clear expectations, and set explicit response-time boundaries
Hand the repository to the stranger immediately; anyone is better than burnout
Delete the repository so nobody depends on unmaintained code
Keep going silently; maintainers do not get to quit
scenarios.why: Bus factor is a governance problem: handing control to an unvetted stranger risks supply-chain compromise of every downstream user, and deleting the repo breaks dependents without warning. The durable fix is shared maintainership built deliberately: documented triage, multiple trusted committers, and boundaries that make the role sustainable.
scenarios.hint: Which option protects downstream users while making your role survivable?

lessons.title: Forge — Core concepts
concepts: Ship small and ship early: a working v0.1 in users' hands teaches more than a perfect v1.0 in your head, and momentum beats polish.
README-driven development: write the README first, including install and quick-start; if you cannot explain it simply, you cannot build it simply.
License before you publish: no license means no rights for users. Pick permissive (MIT/Apache-2.0) for adoption or copyleft deliberately, never accidentally.
Small PRs get reviewed: split refactors, features, and upgrades into independently mergeable units that CI can verify and humans can actually read.
Semantic versioning is a contract with strangers: breaking changes ship as majors with migration notes, because your users' build ranges trust you.
Curate the portfolio: three finished, documented projects prove more than thirty half-built ones; archive or delete the rest.

example.code:
$ git init -b main && git add . && git commit -m "Initial commit"
$ git tag v0.1.0 && git log --oneline -1
a3f9c1d Initial commit
example.walkthrough: The shipping ritual in four commands: initialize, commit, tag. A version tag turns a folder of files into a releasable artifact with a name users can reference and you can never un-ship.

pitfalls: Common trap: no LICENSE file, which legally means 'all rights reserved' and scares off every serious user.
Common trap: giant mixed PRs that no reviewer can actually review, hiding bugs behind green CI.
Common trap: writing the README last, so the quick-start commands have never been copy-pasted by anyone.
Common trap: portfolio sprawl; unfinished repos signal unfinished thinking.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Ship a v0.1
labs.objective: Take a scratch project from folder to tagged v0.1.0 release with license and working quick-start.
steps: Initialize a git repo with a main branch.
Write README.md: one-line description, install, and quick-start commands.
Add a LICENSE file (MIT or Apache-2.0) with your name and year.
Run every quick-start command yourself in a clean directory and fix what breaks.

checks.hint: List tags to confirm v0.1.0 exists.
Confirm a LICENSE file is present in the repo root.

labs.title: Write a reviewable PR
labs.objective: Produce a small, well-described pull request that a stranger could review in ten minutes.
steps: Create a feature branch from main.
Make one focused change: under 200 lines, single purpose.
Write the PR description: what, why, how to test, and screenshots or output.
Self-review the diff and leave at least one comment explaining a non-obvious choice.
Check that CI passes before requesting review.

checks.hint: Keep the diff small and focused; check the stat.

simulations.title: The broken build
simulations.brief: A first-time contributor opened a great PR — and CI is red. They are embarrassed and going quiet. Fix the build without crushing the contributor.

steps.symptom: PR #214 from a new contributor: solid feature, failing tests. The contributor just commented 'sorry, I'll close it.'
evidence:
PR #214 | 3 tests failing: test_total_empty, test_total_floats
Contributor: first PR ever | comment: 'sorry, I'll close it'
options: Let them close it — the tests must pass
Reproduce the failures locally, identify the real cause, and coach them through the fix in the PR
Merge it anyway — the feature works
Rewrite their PR yourself and push to their branch
steps.explain: Red CI on a first PR is a teaching moment, not a rejection. You reproduce, you find the actual cause, and you coach in the open so the contributor learns and stays. Rewriting it yourself teaches them that their work was not worth fixing.

steps.symptom: Reproduced: their total() breaks on empty lists and floats — the tests are right, the code needs two small guards.
evidence:
total([]) -> error (should be 0)
total([1.5, 2.5]) -> 3 (should be 4.0)
Fix: ~4 lines
options: Comment: 'Fix the edge cases' and wait
Point at the exact lines, explain why empty and float inputs matter, and let them write the fix
Push the fix to their branch yourself — faster
Disable the failing tests
steps.explain: Specific, kind, and hands-off the keyboard: show them where, explain why edge cases matter (empty input is the most common real-world input), and let them own the fix. The goal is a contributor who can do the next one alone.

steps.symptom: They fixed it. CI is green. The PR is ready to merge.
evidence:
CI: green | review: approved
Contributor: 'Thanks for the help — that was fun actually'
options: Merge quietly
Merge with a genuine thank-you that names what was good about the work — then invite them to pick up another issue
Ask them to squash, rebase, and re-verify first
Hold the merge until they add more tests
steps.explain: The merge message is culture: name what was good, thank them publicly, and hand them the next rung on the ladder. Contributors who feel seen come back; contributors who feel processed do not.

simulations.debrief: You protected the contributor, taught in the open, and turned a red build into a returning contributor. Maintainers do not just merge code — they grow people.

simulations.title: Merge or close?
simulations.brief: PR #220 is a good feature wrapped in 800 lines of scope creep, drive-by refactors, and a new dependency. The author is a senior engineer who 'just fixed things while in there.' Decide.

steps.symptom: The core feature is 150 lines and excellent. The other 650 lines: refactored helpers, renamed variables, and a new utility library.
evidence:
+812 / -340 lines | core feature: ~150 lines
Extras: refactored helpers, renames, new dep 'quickutil'
Author: senior, 'fixed things while in there'
options: Merge it — the feature is good and the author is senior
Ask for the split: feature in this PR, refactors and the new dependency in follow-ups with their own reviews
Close it — scope creep is disrespectful
Merge and revert the extras yourself later
steps.explain: Review the change you were asked to review. Splitting is not punishment — it is how each change gets the review it deserves, and how the next person can revert the refactor without reverting the feature. Seniority does not exempt anyone from small PRs.

steps.symptom: The author pushes back: 'Splitting will take me all day. Just merge it.'
evidence: Author: 'This is bureaucracy. The code is good.'
options: Cave — they are senior and busy
Hold the line kindly: offer to pair on the split for 30 minutes, and explain the new dependency needs its own security look
Escalate to their manager
Merge but leave a passive-aggressive comment
steps.explain: Standards held with kindness beat standards abandoned for comfort. Offering 30 minutes of pairing turns 'bureaucracy' into teamwork — and the new dependency genuinely needs its own review, which is a technical argument, not a power move.

steps.symptom: Split done: three clean PRs, all merged. The author thanks you.
evidence:
3 PRs merged | dependency reviewed separately
Author: 'Okay, that was actually easier to review myself too'
options: Say nothing — it worked out
Note the win publicly: small PRs reviewed faster and caught a real issue in the refactor
Write a policy banning large PRs
Require all PRs under 200 lines from now on
steps.explain: Reinforce the behavior you want with evidence, not policy. A hard line-count rule would have blocked the original 150-line feature too — judgment scales, rules do not.

simulations.debrief: You split scope without splitting the relationship, held the standard with an offer of help, and reinforced with evidence. Code review is leadership in small doses.

simulations.title: Release day rollback
simulations.brief: The release went out at 10:00. By 10:20, the error rate is climbing and support tickets are landing. You are the release captain. Respond.

steps.symptom: Error rate 1% -> 8% in 20 minutes post-release. The change: a 'small' config tweak bundled with the feature.
evidence:
v2.14.0 deployed 10:00 | errors climbing since 10:05
Suspect: config tweak bundled with feature
Rollback: one command, ~3 min
options: Roll back now — the release is guilty until proven innocent
Forward-fix: patch the config in production
Wait for more data — 8% might stabilize
Blame the config author
steps.explain: A release correlated with errors gets rolled back first and diagnosed second. Rollback is the cheapest, fastest, most reversible action you have — forward-fixing in production is surgery during an earthquake.

steps.symptom: Rolled back at 10:25. Errors flat again. The team wants to re-ship immediately with the config fixed.
evidence:
10:25 rollback complete | errors back to baseline
Team: 'We know the fix, let's re-ship now'
options: Re-ship immediately — the fix is known
Hold the re-ship: reproduce the failure in staging, verify the fix there, then ship on the normal cadence
Ship only the config fix with no review
Cancel the release entirely
steps.explain: The urgency that caused the incident cannot be the urgency that fixes it. Reproduce in staging, verify the fix where it is safe, ship on cadence. 'We know the fix' is exactly what was said about the config tweak.

steps.symptom: Re-shipped cleanly the next day. What changes about the release process?
evidence:
Cause: untested config bundled with feature
Detection: 20 min (user reports beat the alerts)
options: Ban config changes in releases
Unbundle config from code releases, add a canary stage, and alert on error-rate deltas — not user reports
Require VP approval for every release
Go back to monthly releases
steps.explain: Fix the system, not the symptom: config ships separately from code, canaries catch what CI cannot, and alerts should fire before users do. The rollback worked — now make sure you need it less often.

simulations.debrief: You rolled back instead of hero-fixing, resisted the rushed re-ship, and fixed the process that allowed the incident. Release captains are judged by reversibility, not velocity.

simulations.title: The abandoned dependency
simulations.brief: Your most critical service depends on a library whose maintainer just archived the repo: 'no time, thanks all.' A CVE in it drops next week. Work the problem.

steps.symptom: Library 'leftpad-plus' archived by its maintainer. Your auth service depends on it. A CVE affecting it publishes in 7 days.
evidence:
leftpad-plus: archived, single maintainer
Used by: auth service (critical path)
CVE publishes in 7 days | no patch coming upstream
options: Fork it immediately and patch the CVE yourself
First assess: how deep is the dependency, what does it actually do, and can it be replaced or vendored?
Ignore it — archived does not mean broken
Rewrite the auth service from scratch
steps.explain: Assess before you act: a 40-line string helper gets vendored in an afternoon; a deep framework integration needs a real migration plan. Forking first and understanding later leaves you maintaining a fork you did not need.

steps.symptom: Assessment: it is 200 lines, does one thing well, and the CVE is in a code path you actually use. No maintained alternative exists.
evidence:
Size: ~200 lines, single purpose
CVE: in the used code path | alternatives: none maintained
Usage: 3 call sites in auth service
options: Vendor the 200 lines into your repo, patch the CVE, add tests around the vendored code, and document why
Fork the repo and publish your fork as the new official version
Wait for the community to fork it
Pin the vulnerable version and hope
steps.explain: For 200 lines with no alternative, vendoring wins: the code lives in your repo, under your tests, with your patch — no fork-maintenance theater. Document the why so the next person does not 'clean up' the vendored code.

steps.symptom: Vendored and patched. Now protect the rest of the dependency tree.
options: Audit the tree for single-maintainer and archived dependencies, set up vulnerability scanning in CI, and define a policy for adopting new deps
Ban all third-party dependencies
Vendor everything preemptively
Trust that this was a one-off
steps.explain: One abandoned dep is a warning about the tree: audit for bus-factor-one maintainers, scan continuously in CI, and make dependency adoption a conscious decision with criteria. You cannot prevent abandonment — you can prevent surprise.

simulations.debrief: You assessed before forking, vendored surgically with tests, and turned one scare into dependency policy. Supply-chain thinking is maintenance thinking.

simulations.title: First open-source contribution
simulations.brief: You want your first open-source contribution to count — for the project and for your portfolio. Three options are on the table. Choose well.

steps.symptom: Option A: a trendy repo with 40k stars and 300 open PRs. Option B: a small tool you actually use, with 3 friendly maintainers. Option C: starting your own project from zero.
evidence:
A: 40k stars, 300 open PRs, maintainer burnout visible
B: small tool you use daily, 3 active kind maintainers
C: your own project, zero users
options: A — the stars will look great on the resume
B — a used tool with kind maintainers: your PR gets reviewed, merged, and used
C — build your own thing instead
Contribute to all three at once
steps.explain: First contributions should optimize for merged and mentored, not stars. A small project you actually use gives you context, kind reviewers, and a merged PR that real users touch. The 40k-star repo will still be there for contribution number ten.

steps.symptom: You picked B. The issue list has: a typo fix, a confusing error message, and a feature request marked 'help wanted.'
evidence:
#88: typo in README | #91: confusing error message
#94: feature request, 'help wanted', 2 months old
options: The feature — biggest impact for the portfolio
The error message — small, well-scoped, touches real code, and shows you care about users
The typo — safest
All three in one PR
steps.explain: The error-message fix is the sweet spot: real code, clear scope, visible user benefit, and reviewable in one sitting. Typos do not demonstrate much; the stale feature request is probably stale for a reason. Start where you can finish well.

steps.symptom: PR merged. The maintainer thanked you publicly. What goes in the portfolio?
evidence: PR merged | maintainer thanks in the release notes
options: 'Contributed to open source' — keep it vague
Link the merged PR, describe the problem and your fix in two sentences, and note the maintainer's review — evidence, not adjectives
Claim you are a core contributor now
Do not mention it — it was small
steps.explain: Portfolios run on evidence: the linked PR, the problem, the fix, the review. 'Contributed to open source' says nothing; a merged PR with a maintainer's thanks says everything. Small and merged beats big and abandoned.

simulations.debrief: You optimized for merged over famous, scoped for finishable, and documented with evidence. That is how a portfolio gets built: one real contribution at a time.

consoleSims.title: Ship the portfolio update
consoleSims.brief: Your portfolio site needs the new project. Create a branch feat/portfolio, then open a pull request against main with the update.

tasks.hint: Open Branches and create a branch: NAME=feat/portfolio.

tasks.instruction: Open a pull request titled 'Add portfolio project' from feat/portfolio into main.
tasks.hint: Open a PR: TITLE='Add portfolio project', BASE=main, HEAD=feat/portfolio.

consoleSims.debrief: Branch, then PR: the smallest possible shipping loop. Every portfolio update should flow through review, even your own.

consoleSims.title: Review and merge the health check
consoleSims.brief: PR #1 'Add health check endpoint' is reviewed and green. Approve it, then merge it — shipping is a verb.

tasks.hint: On PR #1 (Add health check endpoint), approve it: PR=1.
Merge PR #1 — approve first, then merge.

consoleSims.debrief: Approved and merged. Reviews are not bureaucracy — they are the last cheap place to catch mistakes.

consoleSims.title: Green the pipeline
consoleSims.brief: The pipeline shows a failed test stage. Trigger a fresh build, then retry the test stage — flaky tests get retried, real failures get fixed.

tasks.hint: Trigger a build — resets the stages so you can work them.

consoleSims.debrief: Trigger, retry, observe. CI is a feedback loop — keep it fast and keep it honest.

consoleSims.title: Fix the float bug
consoleSims.brief: A reviewer flagged it: total() in app.py starts its accumulator at int 0, so float inputs lose their type. Open app.py and fix line 2 to start from 0.0.

tasks.instruction: Fix line 2 of app.py to read exactly: four spaces, then 's = 0.0'.
tasks.hint: Fix line 2: FILE=app.py, LINE=2, TEXT='    s = 0.0' (keep the four-space indent).

consoleSims.debrief: Small fix, real review, typed correctly. Most shipped bugs are one-line fixes that nobody reviewed — this one got both.

terminalMissions.title: Who is shipping
terminalMissions.brief: Shipped work has an author. Print your username.
terminalMissions.success_message: Author identified. Ship under your name, proudly.

terminalMissions.title: Name the build machine
terminalMissions.brief: Builds are reproducible from a known machine. Print the hostname.

checks.hint: Run: hostname — name the build machine.

terminalMissions.success_message: Build machine named. "Works on my machine" starts with naming the machine.

terminalMissions.title: List the project
terminalMissions.brief: Before you build, know what you have. List the project directory.
terminalMissions.success_message: Project listed. You cannot build on what you have not looked at.

terminalMissions.title: Confirm the workspace
terminalMissions.brief: Print your working directory — builds run from a known place.
terminalMissions.success_message: Workspace confirmed. Known place, known build.

terminalMissions.title: Tag the release
terminalMissions.brief: Releases get names. Tag this one with echo: v2.14.0.

checks.hint: Run: echo with the release tag (e.g. echo "release v2.14.0").

terminalMissions.success_message: Release tagged. Named releases are retrievable releases.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the builder identity
terminalMissions.brief: Signed releases come from verified builders. Print your full identity record.
terminalMissions.success_message: Builder verified. Ship under a verified name.

terminalMissions.title: Announce the release
terminalMissions.brief: Announce the release with echo, then print the platform string for the release notes.

checks.hint: Run: echo with the announcement (e.g. echo "v2.14.0 is live").
Run: uname -a — record the build platform.

terminalMissions.success_message: Release announced and documented. Shipping is a verb with a record.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
